c.tagline: Andalusia's Moorish jewel — the Alhambra, free tapas, and Sierra Nevada snow.

taxi.fareNote: Metered white taxis are the norm; Uber has only a limited presence, so Cabify and Free Now are the main ride-hail apps. Fixed tariffs apply to and from the airport.

emergency.note: 112 is the EU-wide emergency number connecting to police, fire and ambulance.

hood_landmark.Albaicín: Mirador de San Nicolás with its classic sunset view of the Alhambra
hood_landmark.Sacromonte: cave-house flamenco zambras beneath Sacromonte Abbey
hood_landmark.Realejo: Campo del Príncipe square and the Casa de los Tiros museum

hood_landmark.Alhambra & Mauror: the Alhambra palace-fortress and Generalife gardens

avoid.reason: Pickpocketing around the Alhambra, Albaicín and Sacromonte; caution at night

hood_desc: The old Moorish quarter of steep cobbled lanes, whitewashed carmen houses, and hidden plazas facing the Alhambra; the Mirador de San Nicolás offers the classic sunset view. Best for atmosphere and photogenic wandering.

A hillside of whitewashed cave houses above the Albaicín, the historic Roma quarter and heartland of zambra flamenco, with caves hosting nightly shows. Suits travelers after flamenco and offbeat character.
Granada's former Jewish quarter below the Alhambra, now a lively student and tapas district full of bars, street art, and carmen gardens. Good for nightlife and eating out.
The commercial heart around the Cathedral, Plaza Nueva, and Gran Vía, with shops, the Alcaicería silk-market lanes, and easy transport. The best base for first-timers who want everything walkable.
The wooded hill of the Alhambra and Generalife with quiet leafy lanes, upscale hotels, and the Carmen de los Mártires gardens. Suits those wanting calm and proximity to the monument.
lodging: La Constanza Casa Cueva by ASH

water.note: Tap water from the Sierra Nevada is among Spain's best and safe to drink.

transit.hours: City buses run roughly 6:15 AM to 11 PM, with a reduced night-bus (búho) network; the metro runs about 6:30 AM to 11 PM, later on weekends.
transit.note: Granada's compact centre is best walked; the LAC line links the main hubs and small microbuses (C-lines) climb into the Albaicín and Sacromonte where big buses can't go. A single tram-metro line serves the outskirts and university.
transit.pay: Buy a rechargeable Credibus card for cheaper fares, or pay the driver in cash; the metro uses its own contactless ticket. Contactless bank cards are increasingly accepted.

bus: ALSA intercity coaches from the bus station
train: Renfe AVE high-speed to Madrid, Antequera, Córdoba & Barcelona from Granada station

transit.m: Airport bus (Autocares González) to city centre (~45 min, timed to flights)
Taxi to city centre (fixed tariff, ~20-25 min)

tip.r: Not expected; rounding up or leaving small change for good service is appreciated, and tapas usually come free with drinks.

food.name: Tapas gratis
food.desc: Granada still gives a free tapa with every drink, and the plates get better with each round. Order three drinks on a bar crawl and you have eaten dinner.

places.name: Bodegas Castaneda
places.note: Hanging hams, flamenco posters, barrel vermouth; the classic Granada tapas bar since 1971.

places.name: Bar Los Diamantes
places.note: Fried-fish institution since 1942; the free tapa is a heap of pescaito frito.

places.name: Cerveceria La Riviera
places.note: Famous for the sheer size and variety of its free tapas; students pack it out.

food.name: Tortilla del Sacromonte
food.desc: The gypsy-quarter omelette: eggs bound with lamb brains and sweetbreads, ham, peas and pepper. Rich, offal-forward and unique to Granada.

places.name: Casa Juanillo
places.note: Cave-district restaurant with a terrace over the Alhambra; the traditional Sacromonte address.

places.name: Mirador de Morayma
places.note: Carmen garden restaurant facing the Alhambra; refined version of the offal tortilla.

places.name: Los Manueles
places.area: Plaza de Bib-Rambla / Calle Reyes Catolicos
places.note: Feeding Granada since 1917; purely Andalusian menu with the classic tortilla.

food.name: Habas con jamon
food.desc: Young broad beans from the Vega, fried in olive oil with Trevelez mountain ham and often finished with a soft egg. The most granadino plate there is.

places.name: Los Mascarones
places.note: Friendly locals' bar that specialises in habas con jamon; small, so go early.

places.name: Los Manueles
places.note: House specialty since 1917, served with a fried quail egg on top.

places.name: Bodegas Castaneda
places.note: Standard on the raciones board; order with a caña and stand at the barrel.

food.name: Remojon granadino
food.desc: A winter salad of orange segments, salt cod, black olives, spring onion, hard-boiled egg and a lot of olive oil - Moorish-era cooking still on every menu.

places.name: Bodegas Castaneda
places.note: Traditional remojon on the tapas list, best in citrus season from December to March.

places.name: Taberna La Tana
places.note: Tiny wine-focused taberna; the staff match a Granada wine to the salad for you.

places.name: Los Manueles
places.note: Andalusian standards done properly, remojon among them; tourist-friendly but genuine.

food.name: Berenjenas con miel de cana
food.desc: Aubergine batons fried crisp and drizzled with dark cane molasses from the Motril coast - the sweet-salty tapa Granada is best known for.

places.name: Bar Los Diamantes
places.note: Standing-room fry house; aubergines and pescaito eaten elbow to elbow at the bar.

places.name: Bodegas Castaneda
places.note: Consistently good version with proper Motril cane honey rather than generic syrup.

places.name: Taberna La Tana
places.note: Realejo is the locals' tapas barrio; La Tana is its most-recommended small bar.

food.name: Piononos
food.desc: Two-bite pastries from nearby Santa Fe: syrup-soaked rolled sponge topped with a scorched dome of toasted cream, named after Pope Pius IX.

places.name: Casa Ysla
places.note: The family that invented the pionono in 1897; still the definitive version.

places.name: Pasteleria Lopez-Mezquita
places.note: Century-old city-centre pastry shop; piononos plus Granada's convent sweets.

places.name: Plaza de Bib-Rambla cafes
places.note: Central square where the terrace cafes serve piononos with thick chocolate.

food.name: Vino de la costa
food.desc: Rustic, faintly oxidised wine from the Contraviesa hills and the Alpujarras, poured straight from the barrel. Cheap, local and nothing like a modern Rioja.

places.name: Bodegas Castaneda
places.note: Barrel wines and its own calicasas mix drawn from the vats behind the bar.

places.name: Taberna La Tana
places.note: Small list built around Granada and Andalusian growers; the owner talks you through it.

places.name: Bar Los Diamantes
places.note: Costa wine by the glass with the free fried-fish tapa; the classic Navas crawl stop.

food.name: Cerveza Alhambra
food.desc: Granada has brewed Alhambra since 1925; ask for a caña of Reserva 1925, the maltier bottled lager locals order when they are settling in for the evening.

places.name: Cerveceria La Riviera
places.note: Cold cañas and the biggest free tapas in the centre; loud, cheap, always full.

places.name: Bar Los Diamantes
places.note: Navas is the tapas street; a caña here always arrives with fried fish beside it.

places.name: Bodegas Castaneda
places.note: Draught Alhambra plus vermouth on tap; a good first stop on any tapas route.

landmarks: The Alhambra and Nasrid Palaces
Spain's most visited monument, this hilltop Moorish palace-city of stucco lacework, myrtle courtyards and lion fountains is the crowning glory of Al-Andalus.
Generalife
The sultans' summer estate above the Alhambra weaves cypress avenues, water staircases and rose gardens into a paradise of fountains and views.
Mirador de San Nicolás
The Albaicín's celebrated terrace frames the Alhambra glowing red against the snowy Sierra Nevada, best at sunset with flamenco guitar drifting by.
Albaicín
Granada's UNESCO-listed Moorish quarter tumbles downhill in whitewashed lanes, jasmine-draped cármenes and hidden plazas little changed since Nasrid times.
Granada Cathedral
A luminous Renaissance colossus built over the former great mosque, its soaring white columns and golden chapels announcing Castile's triumph in 1492.
Royal Chapel (Capilla Real)
The flamboyant Gothic mausoleum of Isabella and Ferdinand holds the Catholic Monarchs' marble tombs, crowns and an exquisite Flemish art collection.
Sacromonte
The old Roma quarter's whitewashed cave houses stage intimate zambra flamenco by night, with the Sacromonte Abbey crowning the valley above.
Carrera del Darro and Paseo de los Tristes
Arguably Spain's most romantic street follows the Darro river beneath the Alhambra past stone bridges, convents and the 11th-century El Bañuelo baths.
Monastery of Cartuja
Behind a sober facade erupts Spain's most delirious Baroque interior, a sacristy of swirling stucco dubbed the 'Christian Alhambra'.
Alcaicería
The rebuilt Moorish silk bazaar's narrow alleys beside the cathedral brim with lanterns, taracea marquetry and spice stalls echoing Granada's souk past.

train.note: No international trains. AVE high-speed services reach Madrid in about 3h15 via Antequera, with connections to Córdoba and Barcelona, plus regional Avant and media-distancia trains to Almería and other Andalusian towns. The station sits northwest of the centre, about 20 minutes' walk or a short bus ride from the cathedral. Booking opens around 60 days ahead.

bus.note: No international coaches start in Granada; those run from Madrid, Málaga or Seville. ALSA (https://www.alsa.com/en) runs frequently from the Estación de Autobuses on the northern edge of town to Málaga (about 1h45), Seville (3 hours), Córdoba and Madrid (4h30), plus seasonal buses up to the Sierra Nevada ski resort. Bus 33 links the terminal with the centre.

ferry.note: Granada is inland at the foot of the Sierra Nevada with no port, so there are no ferries. The nearest sailings are from Motril on the coast about an hour south, which has seasonal crossings to Melilla and Nador in Morocco.

half.name: Sierra Nevada
half.blurb: Mainland Spain's highest peaks, about 45 minutes up the road — skiing and snow in winter, high-mountain hiking toward Mulhacén in summer.

half.name: Guadix
half.blurb: A striking town an hour east famous for its inhabited cave houses and cathedral, set amid dramatic badland scenery.

full.name: The Alpujarras
full.blurb: White villages like Pampaneira, Bubión and Capileira strung across the southern slopes of the Sierra Nevada, known for crafts and cured ham.

full.name: Córdoba
full.blurb: Home of the extraordinary Mezquita mosque-cathedral, about 2 hours northwest by road or fast train.

full.name: Nerja & Frigiliana
full.blurb: Costa del Sol beaches, the Balcón de Europa and the whitewashed hill village of Frigiliana, around 1h30 south.
